topic.title: The ₹350 chair
topic.claim: Half of what you pay for café coffee is rent on a chair, because our cities have almost nowhere free to sit.
topic.moment: You buy a cold coffee you don't want so you can take a call for an hour.

turn.actually: We're paying for a seat, a plug and Wi-Fi, with the coffee as the ticket.

topic.feeling: Like I'm paying an entry fee to exist in my own city.
topic.villain: Cities with almost no free public places to sit: few libraries, parks or plazas
topic.because: When the only places to sit are ones that sell something, the café can price the seat. The menu is just how it bills you.
topic.payoff: Would you buy that coffee if you could sit in a park with Wi-Fi? Then you know what you paid for.
topic.behaviour: People work, date and take calls from cafés, buying one drink per hour as rent.
topic.mechanism: Scarce free space lets private places charge for sitting.
topic.group: Young professionals in metros, often in shared flats
topic.send_to: The friend who 'works from a café' three days a week
topic.why_now: Hybrid work has filled cafés with laptops on weekdays.
real_details: A r/hyderabad post says the poster doesn't want more cafes and wants clean parks and public spaces instead. The thread text includes no comments, numbers or personal stories.

score.why: The café coffee is the ticket for a chair. Cities with nowhere free to sit explain it, and the line reads as an everyday observation, not a complaint.

notes: The take's premise is wrong: Slide 7 says 'A café doesn't care what the chair costs… Your ₹300 isn't repaying the chair.' The 17% figure is roughly right as a reported number: FY25 rent was ₹55.2 Cr on ₹325.4 Cr of operating revenue, about 17%. The conclusion drawn from it does not follow, for three reasons. (1) A 17% rent line is one of a café chain's biggest costs. Rent was 14.3% of total expenses, sitting alongside ₹94 Cr of staff costs. (2) That revenue includes sales of coffee products (beans and retail), not just café orders, so rent as a share of café takings is likely higher than 17%. Lease costs can also be booked partly as depreciation instead of rent. The FY26 rent line fell to ₹26.65 Cr while depreciation nearly doubled to ₹87 Cr, which suggests that is happening here, though the reports don't explain it. (3) Blue Tokai lost ₹50 Cr in FY25 and ₹83 Cr in FY26. Its ₹300 drinks are not even covering its costs, so the price cannot be floating free of what the space costs.. How it actually works: Café menu prices start from costs: ingredients, staff, and occupancy (rent, fit-out, power), with occupancy usually a double-digit share of revenue. Prices are then pushed up to whatever customers will pay at that location. Customers' other options, including having nowhere else to sit, do shape what they will pay, but the price still has to cover the cost of the seat over time, and a loss-making chain like Blue Tokai shows that today's ₹300 doesn't yet. Rebuild the post on the correct mechanism.

_ledger.text:
[cover] Your café cold coffee is really [a ticket to a chair]
The drink is the excuse. The table is the product.
 

[slide 1] Your ₹300 cold coffee isn't the thing you're buying. It's a ticket to a chair, a plug and Wi-Fi.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] You didn't even want a cold coffee. You wanted a table, a socket and one quiet hour for a work call.

[slide 3] You find the plug before you find the menu. And the milk steamer still goes off the second your call connects.

[slide 4] Walk into any Starbucks or Third Wave on a weekday:
– a laptop on every table, one drink each
– a first date that couldn't happen at either home
– someone on a call because the flatmate is home

[slide 5] And when your cup has been empty too long, you order a cookie you won't eat. Rent's due.

[slide 6] Because our cities have almost nowhere free to sit. Libraries are rare, and benches with shade are a luxury.
So every chair outside home comes with a menu. The café's rival isn't the café next door. It's your bedroom.

[slide 7] A café doesn't care what the chair costs. It cares where you could go.
Rent is only about 17% of what Blue Tokai takes in. Your ₹300 isn't repaying the chair.
It's priced against the flat with the flatmate on speaker.

[slide 8] I don't hate cafés for it. I've taken more calls over coffee I didn't want than I'd like to admit.
If you don't have a spare room, the café is where you work, date and get some air.

[slide 9] But if you're one of three people in a 2BHK, or in a PG with no common room, this hits harder.
For them, ₹300 an hour is the entry fee to step out of their own room.

[slide 10] Picture a shaded bench with free Wi-Fi down your lane.
Would you still order the cold coffee?
If not, that ₹300 was rent.

[end card] Read it again the next time you order a second drink just so the waiter stops hovering.
Send to the friend who 'works from a café' three days a week and calls it a coffee habit.

[caption] When you're working from a café, the coffee is just how they bill you for the chair, the plug and the Wi-Fi.

Our cities have almost nowhere free to sit, so every seat outside home comes with a menu.

"Chal, café mein baith ke kaam karte hain" usually means "ghar pe jagah nahi hai."

Send this to the friend who 'works from a café' three days a week and still calls it a coffee habit.

4e349e7104fdec0e32cc5498f383ec336fd8585f.broken_premise: Slide 7 says 'A café doesn't care what the chair costs… Your ₹300 isn't repaying the chair.' The 17% figure is roughly right as a reported number: FY25 rent was ₹55.2 Cr on ₹325.4 Cr of operating revenue, about 17%. The conclusion drawn from it does not follow, for three reasons. (1) A 17% rent line is one of a café chain's biggest costs. Rent was 14.3% of total expenses, sitting alongside ₹94 Cr of staff costs. (2) That revenue includes sales of coffee products (beans and retail), not just café orders, so rent as a share of café takings is likely higher than 17%. Lease costs can also be booked partly as depreciation instead of rent. The FY26 rent line fell to ₹26.65 Cr while depreciation nearly doubled to ₹87 Cr, which suggests that is happening here, though the reports don't explain it. (3) Blue Tokai lost ₹50 Cr in FY25 and ₹83 Cr in FY26. Its ₹300 drinks are not even covering its costs, so the price cannot be floating free of what the space costs.
4e349e7104fdec0e32cc5498f383ec336fd8585f.actual_mechanism: Café menu prices start from costs: ingredients, staff, and occupancy (rent, fit-out, power), with occupancy usually a double-digit share of revenue. Prices are then pushed up to whatever customers will pay at that location. Customers' other options, including having nowhere else to sit, do shape what they will pay, but the price still has to cover the cost of the seat over time, and a loss-making chain like Blue Tokai shows that today's ₹300 doesn't yet.

sources.quote: Blue Tokai's rent costs stood at INR 55.2 Cr in FY25, up 67% from INR 33 Cr in FY24. It accounted for 14.3% of the total expenses.
Employee benefit expenses also rose 24% year-on-year to Rs 94 crore in FY25... reduced its losses by 20.6% to Rs 50 crore in FY25, from Rs 63 crore in FY24.
Rent expenses rose 59.6% to Rs 26.65 crore... depreciation nearly doubled to Rs 87 crore... its net losses widened 53.7% to Rs 83 crore from Rs 54 crore.
